title: What role does breast density play?
intro: Breast density describes how much of the breast is made up of glandular and connective tissue compared with fat, as seen on a mammogram. Dense breasts are common and normal. Density matters because it can make cancers harder to see and is itself linked to a slightly higher risk of breast cancer.

sections.heading: What density means
paragraphs: On a mammogram, fat looks dark, while glandular and fibrous tissue looks white. Breasts are often grouped into four categories, from mostly fatty to extremely dense. Density is not related to how breasts feel, or to their size, and it cannot be judged by touch. It is more common in younger women and tends to decrease with age and after menopause.

sections.heading: Why it matters
paragraphs: Dense tissue and tumours both appear white on a mammogram, so cancers can be hidden, which lowers the sensitivity of mammography. Women with very dense breasts also have a higher risk of breast cancer than women with fatty breasts, but density is only one of many risk factors, such as age, family history and genes.

sections.heading: Additional tests
paragraphs: For women with dense breasts, additional imaging such as ultrasound or magnetic resonance imaging may find more cancers, but also leads to more false alarms and extra tests. Whether additional tests are offered differs between countries and guidelines, and the benefit for survival is still being studied. Discuss the options with your doctor.

sections.heading: What you can do
paragraphs: Take part in recommended screening, know your breasts and report changes such as a lump, skin changes, nipple discharge or pain, even after a normal mammogram. Reduce modifiable risks such as excess alcohol, being overweight after menopause and lack of activity. Density cannot be changed on purpose.

sections.heading: Being informed
paragraphs: In some countries women are told their density after a mammogram. If yours is high, ask what it means for you, whether your risk is increased and whether extra tests make sense. Having dense breasts is not a disease, and does not mean you will develop cancer.

examples.title: Asking about density
examples.text: Imagine your mammogram report mentions dense breasts. You could ask your doctor whether extra imaging is suitable for you.

examples.title: Noticing a change
examples.text: Suppose you feel a new lump after a normal mammogram. You might see your doctor promptly rather than waiting for the next screening.
